extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and empirical economists studying historical inequality (Great Depression / New Deal era)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating empirical measures and regressions of inequality across cities/counties during the Great Contraction and the 1930s (income ginis, housing ginis, and top-end taxpayer shares), including data concordances, regression specification, instrumentation, and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Income gini based on family incomes (Mendershausen data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Income gini based on family incomes in 1929 for 33 cities and in 1933 for up to 48 cities (Mendershausen data used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family income measures include relief transfers (so relief spending can directly affect the family income gini). Nearly every income gini rose between 1929 and 1933; regressions of changes show inequality more likely to increase where state per capita personal income fell most. Use these income ginis to capture distributional changes across the full income distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housing gini using contract rents and implicit rents for homeowners
rubrics_metrics.description: Gini coefficients calculated from contract rents for renters and implicit rents (1/100th of home values) for homeowners reported in Census/housing surveys (7 nominal housing-value bins and corresponding 7 rent bins; also a 5-bin concordance for smaller cities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit rents are converted by Census at 1/100th of home value; implied discount rates vary with assumed home life (e.g., 11.54% for 30-year, 10.3% for 20-year, 8.4% for 15-year, 3.4% for 10-year). Housing ginis allow expanding sample (up to 955 cities or more) and moving earlier in time, but mixing implicit rents for homeowners and contract rents understates inequality because it treats homeowners like renters without giving extra value for holding housing wealth. 5-bin ginis tend to imply greater inequality by about 0.03 than 7-bin ginis. Consider alternative concordances and adjustments for homeowners when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-end inequality measure: share (number) of federal taxpayers per family
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of top-end inequality given by the number (or share) of federal income taxpayers per family in a county.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures the number of households with incomes above federal thresholds (nationwide fewer than 10%); advantage: available for all counties (large sample expansion). Disadvantage: misses most of the lower 90% of the distribution and is sensitive to tax-rule and rate changes. Better used for cross-sectional comparisons within a year or short panels where tax rules are stable. E.g., use 1939 share to compare with 1940 housing gini to avoid 1940 tax-rule changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of categorical bin concordances to compute gini
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute gini coefficients from reported discrete bins (housing value bins or rent bins) using the categories provided by Census/surveys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For cities >10,000 the Census reported seven nominal value bins; for smaller cities a 5-bin grouping may be used to increase sample. Be aware that the number of bins and concordance choices affect measured gini levels and comparisons across samples (5-bin tends to be higher by ~0.03). Report and test sensitivity to alternative concordances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of timing and survey differences between housing and income data
rubrics_metrics.description: Housing information is based on the situation in March (e.g., March 1934) while income information is retrospective for the most recent full year (e.g., 1933).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing housing and income ginis, account for timing mismatches; this can affect correlations and inferences about changes. Mention timing explicitly and interpret correlations cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read coefficients as elasticities when variables are logged
rubrics_metrics.description: When regressions use natural logs for dependent and independent variables, coefficients can be read as elasticities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports regressions with all variables in logs and interprets statistically significant coefficients as elasticities (note magnitude interpretation and small absolute values observed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include demographic and economic correlates in gini regressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Control variables used include annual manufacturing earnings, county population, percent foreign-born, percent black, percent illiterate, age-share groups (e.g., 30-34, 65-74), and percent urban.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These correlates are included both in level regressions (1930 and 1940) and difference regressions (changes 1930–1940). Expectation examples: higher manufacturing earnings, larger population, higher foreign-born share associated with lower housing inequality; higher illiteracy associated with more inequality. Report elasticities and statistical significance for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for percent urban when county-level correlates are used for cities
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a measure of percent urban in regressions because correlates are measured at the county level and cities may have populations outside city limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using county-level data for city analysis requires controlling for urban share to account for surrounding non-city populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use OLS on levels and OLS on differences (first-differences) to address unobserved fixed factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Run OLS regressions of gini levels on levels of correlates (1930, 1940) and OLS of differences in ginis on differences in correlates across the decade to control for unmeasured and unchanging aspects of cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difference specification helps mitigate omitted variables bias from unchanging city attributes; compare level and difference results to assess robustness and selection biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation caution about selection bias in New Deal program placement
rubrics_metrics.description: New Deal funds were distributed non-randomly — governments chose to spend more in areas where unemployment rose and the economy deteriorated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates bi-directional relationships: relief spending might be higher where inequality rose, confounding causal interpretation. Regression patterns that show positive relationships between per capita relief and increases in gini likely reflect such selection. Use instrumentation or robustness checks and interpret coefficients cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument per-capita relief spending using political/electoral instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed instruments include presence of a Democratic governor in 1928, percent Democrat in the upper house of the state legislature, mean presidential Democratic vote share 1896–1928, and the standard deviation of that share (willingness of voters to swing). Other instruments tried: representation on House Agricultural Committee, distance to simulated HOLC offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report first-stage F-statistics to assess instrument strength (example: F = 4.91 flagged as not particularly strong). Weak first-stage F leads to imprecise and possibly biased IV estimates; discuss instrument plausibility and potential weak-instrument problems. Even with high first-stage F for some instruments (e.g., 34.7 for AAA), final-stage t-statistics may remain small if instruments cannot identify individual program effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and evaluate instrument strength using first-stage F-statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: First-stage F-statistics indicate instrument strength (example values reported: 4.91 for political instruments; other Fs: 7.35 for public works, 13.39 for relief, 34.7 for AAA, 9.35 for HOLC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize conventional thresholds (e.g., F>10) for weak-instrument concerns; low F suggests instruments are weak and final IV estimates may be unreliable. Discuss possible weak-instrument problems and inability to separately identify program effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report robust standard errors where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use robust standard errors in regressions (example: regression with robust standard errors of change in income gini on change in housing gini).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust SEs are used to account for heteroskedasticity; state them explicitly in tables and interpret t-statistics accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine correlations among different inequality measures before substituting
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute correlations between housing ginis, income ginis, and taxpayer-share measures across cities and over time (levels correlations ~0.8; changes correlations ~0.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High correlations justify partial substitution, but discordant mean changes (e.g., income ginis rose while housing ginis mostly fell) indicate the measures do not tell the same story for changes. Use regressions (e.g., change in income gini on change in housing gini) to quantify bias/intercept differences and slopes; do not assume interchangeability without sensitivity checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for tax-rule and tax-rate changes when using taxpayer measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Tax thresholds and rates changed over the 1930s (e.g., major rate increases June 1932 and further changes 1934, 1940), which affect comparability of taxpayer-share measures across periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit use of taxpayer-share as a time-comparable measure to periods with stable tax rules (short panels) or adjust comparisons appropriately (e.g., use 1939 taxpayers for comparisons with 1940 housing gini to avoid 1940 tax-rule changes). Discuss likely effects on tax avoidance and measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use county-level regressions to expand sample for taxpayer-share analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Because taxpayer-share is available for all counties, regressions can be estimated on county samples (including rural counties) to increase observations (e.g., sample >3000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All variables should be measured at county level when expanding sample. Interpret demographic correlates using 1930 Census levels when short-run changes are studied (e.g., 1929–1931 change regression uses 1930 levels for demographics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about expected sign and magnitude of program elasticities and selection effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss theoretical expectations for each New Deal program (e.g., relief expected to lower gini; public works to help middle distribution; HOLC and FHA to favor homeowners and thus potentially increase housing gini).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare empirical signs to expectations: e.g., observed positive relationship between HOLC/FHA activity and housing gini fits expectation because programs favor homeowners; negative AAA elasticity may reflect negative selection of AAA grants into counties with lower inequality in 1930. Interpret magnitudes (most program elasticities small, <0.03) and statistical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct sensitivity/robustness checks: alternative concordances, different samples and data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan to redo housing inequality measures using universal censuses (1930 and 1940) to test how much housing ginis change when altering concordances between home values and implicit rents and to extend analysis to rural areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare results across alternative concordances (5-bin vs 7-bin), sample expansions (more cities/counties), and different outcome measures (income, housing, occupational distributions) to assess robustness and extend time coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge measurement limitations when combining renters and homeowners
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing implicit rents from owned housing with rents paid by tenants treats homeowners like renters in flow measures, which likely understates inequality if housing is seen as a wealth measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If housing gini is used as a proxy for wealth inequality, consider giving homeowners extra value for holding housing wealth or at least discuss the potential understatement and its implications for comparisons with income ginis.
